title: Keep your word, starting with your word to Allah.
subtitle: A surah that opens with a promise kept
then: This surah came after the treaty of Hudaibiyah, when keeping agreements mattered for a whole community. A man once asked Ibn Mas'ud for advice. He said: {idea}when you hear O you who believe, give it your full attention.{/idea} Ibn Abbas said these obligations are {reward}what Allah permitted, forbade and set limits for.{/reward}
now: You said you would call back. You told your friend you would be at the wedding. You clicked I agree on the terms at work. {trap}Small promises slip first.{/trap} The verse puts all of them under one word: fulfill.
old: A promise is serious only when it is written and signed.
new: Every word I give is a contract, and keeping it is part of my faith.
try: Think of one small promise you made this week and have not kept. Keep it today.

title: They blocked you once. Do not let that make you unjust.
subtitle: Hatred is not a license to cross the line

key.label: What your anger is allowed to do

row.title: stay just
sub: your hurt does not move the line

then: In 6 AH the Prophet ﷺ set out with about 1400 Muslims for Umrah, and {trap}Quraysh stopped them from reaching the Sacred Mosque.{/trap} Many pilgrims later had to pass through Muslim land on their way to Makkah. The verse told the believers {idea}not to block them in revenge{/idea}, and to work together only on what is good.
now: The colleague who took credit for your project now needs your sign-off. The relative who skipped your wedding asks for a favor. {trap}You finally have the power to pay it back.{/trap} The verse says: {idea}your old wound does not get a vote.{/idea}
old: If someone wronged me, I am allowed to treat them a little worse.
new: What they did to me does not change what is right for me to do.
try: Think of one person you are quietly waiting to pay back. Do one fair thing for them instead.

title: The religion is complete, and mercy is built into it.
subtitle: A list of limits that ends in a gift and an exception
then: Ibn Kathir explains that these foods were forbidden for {trap}the harm they cause, to body and to faith.{/trap} Qatadah said people before Islam would beat an animal with sticks and eat it once it died. Right after the list, the verse announces {idea}the religion perfected and the favor completed{/idea}, and ends with mercy for anyone forced by hunger.
now: You flip a coin, check a horoscope app, or wait for a sign before a big choice. {trap}Arrows in a new shape.{/trap} The verse says you are not left guessing: {idea}the guidance is already complete{/idea}, and the door for hard situations is already open.
old: Religion is a long list of things I am not allowed to have.
new: It is a finished gift from Someone who already made room for my hardest days.
try: Before one decision today, skip the luck charm or app. Ask Allah for good and choose with a calm heart.

title: They asked what is allowed. The answer: all that is good.
subtitle: Starting from the good, and saying His name over it

row.title: the good is open
sub: the limits are few, and named

then: The companions asked what they could eat. The answer begins with {reward}all good things{/reward}, even game caught by trained hunting animals, as Allah taught them. The Prophet ﷺ taught his young stepson Umar bin Abi Salamah: {idea}say Allah's name, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is in front of you.{/idea}
now: Lunch at your desk, eyes on the phone, food gone before you tasted it. Or dinner at home where everyone reaches across the table. {idea}A name said before the first bite{/idea} turns an ordinary meal into a moment of remembering.
old: Eating is just fuel. Nothing to think about.
new: Every meal starts from a wide permission, and His name makes it a moment with Him.
try: At your next meal, say Bismillah slowly and eat the first three bites without your phone.

title: Your food is lawful to them, and theirs to you.
subtitle: A shared table and fair dealing with neighbors
then: After listing what is forbidden, the verse widens the table: the food of the People of the Scripture is lawful, and {idea}you may feed them from yours.{/idea} Ibn Kathir calls this {reward}equal compensation and fair treatment.{/reward} The verse ends with a sober line: faith is what gives deeds their worth.
now: The neighbor knocks with a plate of food on a holiday. The coworker brings cake for the team. {idea}You get to answer kindness with kindness.{/idea} The plate goes back to their door, never empty.
old: I accept what others offer, but I owe them nothing.
new: A shared table is a two-way street, and fairness goes both directions.
try: Return a kindness today: a plate, a message, a small gift for someone who gave you something.

title: Allah does not want hardship for you. He wants you clean.
subtitle: Washing before prayer, and ease when water is gone

row.title: purity and favor
sub: so that you may be grateful

then: Ibn Kathir notes that the washing begins with intention, citing the hadith: {idea}actions are judged by their intentions.{/idea} On the Day of Victory the Prophet ﷺ prayed five prayers with one washing, and told Umar he did it on purpose. When water runs out, {reward}clean earth is enough.{/reward}
now: You are in a hospital corridor, or a train, or a long shift with no sink nearby. {trap}It feels like prayer is out of reach today.{/trap} The verse says {reward}Allah does not want hardship for you.{/reward} The way back is always made possible.
old: If I cannot do it perfectly, I should not do it at all.
new: He made a way for every situation, because He wants me to come, not to struggle.
try: At your next washing for prayer, slow down and make the intention in your heart first.

title: You once said: we hear and we obey. Remember it.
subtitle: The pledge you made, and the One who sees inside
then: Ibn Kathir says this was the pledge the companions gave when they embraced Islam: {idea}to hear and obey, when they felt active and when they did not.{/idea} The verse reminds them of that favor and that promise, and that {trap}Allah knows what is inside the chest.{/trap}
now: The day you first prayed for real. The Ramadan night you cried and promised to change. {trap}Months later it feels far away.{/trap} The verse does not scold. It says: {idea}remember what you said, and remember who heard it.{/idea}
old: That promise was a moment of emotion. Life moved on.
new: The promise is still mine, and the One I made it to still remembers it.
try: Recall one promise you made to Allah in a strong moment. Do one small part of it today.

title: Be just even to the people you cannot stand.
subtitle: Justice that does not depend on how you feel
then: An-Nu'man bin Bashir's father gave him a gift and asked the Prophet ﷺ to witness it. The Prophet ﷺ asked if every child had received the same. He had not. The Prophet ﷺ said: {idea}fear Allah and treat your children equally{/idea}, and {trap}I will not be a witness to injustice.{/trap}
now: The family group chat is splitting over an old argument. You know your cousin has a point, but you cannot stand him. {trap}Silence feels safer.{/trap} The verse asks you to {idea}stand up for the truth, even when it helps someone you dislike.{/idea}
old: I can be fair to people who treat me well.
new: Justice is owed to everyone, and that is what brings me close to Allah.
try: Say one fair, true thing today about someone you dislike, even if only in your own heart.

title: A promise of forgiveness and a great reward.
subtitle: Deeds are the path, mercy is the gate

row.title: His mercy
sub: deeds are the road to it

then: Right after the call to be just, comes a promise. Ibn Kathir explains that people will not enter Paradise by their actions alone, but {reward}by Allah's mercy and favor.{/reward} Good deeds are {idea}the cause and path that lead to His mercy.{/idea} So all thanks are due to Him.
now: You keep a mental score: prayers done, charity given, days missed. {trap}Some days the score looks bad and you want to quit.{/trap} The verse speaks of forgiveness first. {idea}Your deeds are a road, not a receipt.{/idea}
old: I will only be saved if my good outweighs my bad by enough.
new: My deeds are the road, and His mercy is the gate at its end.
try: After your next prayer, thank Allah for one good deed He made easy for you.

title: Turning away from the signs has an end too.
subtitle: The other side of the promise, stated plainly
then: Verse 9 gave a promise. This verse states the other road in one line. Ibn Kathir says it shows {idea}Allah's perfect justice, wisdom and judgment{/idea}: He is never wrong. Promise and warning stand {trap}side by side so no one is surprised.{/trap}
now: A reminder in a friend's message. A verse that stops you during a scroll. {trap}You swipe past without thinking.{/trap} This verse is not about someone else. {idea}It asks what you do with the signs that reach you.{/idea}
old: Warnings are for other people who are far worse than me.
new: The signs reach me too, and how I respond is what counts.
try: Next time a reminder reaches you today, pause for ten seconds before moving on.

title: Hands reached out to harm you, and Allah held them back.
subtitle: Remembering the harm that never arrived
then: Jabir reported that the Prophet ﷺ rested under a tree and hung his sword on it. A bedouin man took the sword, raised it and asked: who can protect you from me? {idea}The Prophet ﷺ answered: Allah.{/idea} The man lowered the sword, and {reward}the Prophet ﷺ did not punish him.{/reward}
now: The car that braked just in time. The scan that came back clear. The plan against you at work that fell apart before you even heard of it. {idea}Most of the harm you were saved from, you never saw.{/idea}
old: Bad things that did not happen are not worth thinking about.
new: Every harm that missed me is a favor to remember, and a reason to rely on Him.
try: Write down one close call from your life and thank Allah for it by name.

title: I am with you, if you keep your side.
subtitle: A covenant with twelve leaders and a clear offer
then: Allah took a pledge from the Children of Israel through twelve leaders, one for each tribe. Ibn Kathir notes that on the night of Aqabah, {idea}twelve leaders of the Ansar{/idea} also gave the pledge to the Prophet ﷺ for their people. The offer was the same: {reward}I am with you{/reward}, if you pray, give and support the truth.
now: You are the one your family calls when things fall apart. Or the one who leads the team meeting. {idea}Leadership starts with keeping your own promise first.{/idea} The verse says His support travels with the one who keeps his side.
old: Allah is with me no matter what I do.
new: He offers to be with me, and my prayer, charity and loyalty are my side of it.
try: Give a small amount in charity today, quietly, as your part of the pledge.

title: Broken promises harden hearts. Pardon anyway.
subtitle: What breaking a covenant does inside a person
then: Right after the offer of verse 12, this verse tells what happened when the pledge was broken: {trap}hearts grew hard, words were twisted, and parts of the reminder were forgotten.{/trap} Yet the Prophet ﷺ is told: {idea}pardon them and overlook.{/idea}
now: You skip the prayer once and it hurts. By the tenth time you feel nothing. {trap}That numbness is the hardening.{/trap} And when someone breaks a promise to you, the verse still asks you to {idea}pardon and do good.{/idea}
old: Breaking small promises does not change who I am.
new: Each broken promise hardens me a little, and pardoning others softens me back.
try: Pardon one person today for a small broken promise. Tell them, or just let it go in your heart.

title: Forget part of the reminder, and people turn on each other.
subtitle: What happens to a community that drops the core
then: Like verse 13, this is about a covenant taken and {trap}part of the reminder forgotten.{/trap} The result was not punishment from outside, but {trap}enmity and hatred among themselves.{/trap} Allah will tell each one what they used to do.
now: The family that stopped eating together. The mosque committee that argues about everything except the reason it exists. {idea}When the shared core is forgotten, small things become wars.{/idea} The question is what part of the reminder you have let slip.
old: Our fights are about the other person being difficult.
new: Division often begins when we forget what we were reminded of together.
try: Bring back one shared good habit with family or friends this week, like a meal or a prayer together.

title: He made much clear, and let much pass.
subtitle: A light and a clear Book, delivered with restraint
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the Prophet ﷺ made clear what had been hidden or changed, and {reward}passed over much of it, since explaining it would bring no benefit.{/reward} With him came {idea}a light and a clear Book{/idea} for all people.
now: Your friend's story has a few errors. Your coworker's report has small mistakes. {trap}You want to correct every one in front of everyone.{/trap} The verse shows another way: {idea}say what matters, and let the rest go.{/idea}
old: Being truthful means pointing out every mistake I see.
new: Truth is clarity on what matters, with mercy on what does not.
try: Next time you notice a small mistake in someone today, let it pass without comment.

title: Seek His pleasure and you are led to paths of peace.
subtitle: From many darknesses into one light
then: This continues verse 15: the light and the clear Book. Ibn Kathir says the paths of peace are {reward}ways of safety and righteousness{/reward}, and that Allah {idea}brings people out of darkness into light{/idea}, rescuing them from ruin and showing them the clearest path.
now: Three in the morning, too many worries at once: money, health, a falling-out. {trap}Darkness comes in layers.{/trap} The verse says the light is one, and {idea}the door to it is wanting what pleases Him.{/idea}
old: I need to solve all my problems before I can feel at peace.
new: Peace begins when I turn toward what pleases Him, and He leads me out.
try: Tonight before sleep, ask Allah for guidance in one worry by name.

title: Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Him alone.
subtitle: No created being shares the Creator's place
then: The verse answers a claim about Isa, son of Maryam. Ibn Kathir explains it by reminding of {idea}Allah's perfect power over everything.{/idea} Who could stop Him? {reward}All things in existence are His property and creation.{/reward}
now: A favorite scholar, a parent, a doctor, a celebrity. You may never call anyone a god, but {trap}you can still hang your whole heart on a person.{/trap} The verse puts every creature, however loved, {idea}under His dominion.{/idea}
old: The people I admire most could never let me down.
new: Every person I admire is a creation of Allah, and He alone holds everything.
try: Think of one person you depend on too much. Ask Allah directly for what you usually ask them.

title: Being loved is not a pass. You are still accountable.
subtitle: No group label replaces your own deeds
then: Some among the People of the Book said they were Allah's children and beloved. Ibn Kathir explains the reply: {idea}you are human beings like the rest of the children of Adam.{/idea} Allah is Lord of all, and {trap}none can escape His judgment.{/trap}
now: You come from a religious family. Your father is an imam. You go to the right mosque. {trap}It is easy to feel safe by association.{/trap} The verse turns the question back to you: {idea}what are you doing with it?{/idea}
old: Because of where I come from, I am already among the good ones.
new: I am a human being like everyone else, and my deeds return to Allah with me.
try: Do one good deed today that no one would expect from your background or your label.

title: After a long silence, a messenger came. No excuse remains.
subtitle: Good news and warning, delivered when most needed
then: Ibn Kathir reports from Salman Al-Farisi that about {trap}six hundred years passed between Isa and Muhammad ﷺ{/trap} with no messenger. The world was full of confusion. Sending the Prophet ﷺ then was {reward}the perfect favor, when he was needed most.{/reward}
now: You know more about Islam than most people in history ever could. The Quran is in your pocket. {trap}The excuse that no one told me does not fit anymore.{/trap} {idea}The message has arrived, with good news first.{/idea}
old: I did not grow up knowing much, so I cannot be expected to act on it.
new: The message has reached me now, with good news and a warning, and that is a gift.
try: Read one verse today with its meaning, slowly, as if it were just delivered to you.

title: Remember the favors. You are richer than you think.
subtitle: Musa counts his people's blessings before the hard test
then: Before asking his people to move forward, Musa reminded them of {reward}Allah's favors on them.{/reward} Ibn Abbas said made you kings means {idea}having a house, a wife and a servant.{/idea} A hadith says that whoever wakes healthy, safe in his family, with food for the day, has been given the world.
now: You woke up today. Your body works. Your family is safe. There is food in the fridge. {trap}Yet you scroll and feel poor.{/trap} By the measure in this verse, {idea}you are living like a king.{/idea}
old: I will feel blessed once I have more than I have now.
new: A safe home, health and today's food already make me rich.
try: Before your next meal, name three things you have that make you a king by this measure.

title: Go forward into what was promised. Turning back is the loss.
subtitle: Musa calls his people to the next step
then: Ibn Kathir explains that Musa ordered his people to enter the Holy Land and {reward}promised them victory if they went forward.{/reward} The land had been promised to the believers among them. The warning was clear: {trap}turning back would make them losers.{/trap}
now: The course you signed up for and then stopped attending. The apology you drafted and never sent. {trap}Walking away feels safe in the moment.{/trap} The verse says {idea}the loss is in turning back, not in the step forward.{/idea}
old: If I do not try, at least I cannot fail.
new: Turning back from what Allah opened for me is itself the failure.
try: Pick one good thing you abandoned halfway. Take one small step back toward it today.

title: We will go in once it gets easy.
subtitle: The excuse that waits for the obstacle to vanish

row.title: I will, once it is easy

then: Ibn Kathir says their excuse was that the people in the town were {trap}mighty, strong and huge{/trap}, and they could not stand against them. So they set a condition: {trap}we will enter once they leave.{/trap} They wanted the promise without the step.
now: I will start praying when work calms down. I will give charity after the loan is paid. I will fix things with my brother once he calls first. {trap}Waiting for the giants to leave.{/trap} {idea}They rarely leave on their own.{/idea}
old: I will do the right thing once the obstacles are gone.
new: The obstacle is part of the test, not a reason to wait.
try: Name one good thing you keep postponing until it gets easier. Do two minutes of it today.

title: Two men said: go through the gate, and rely on Allah.
subtitle: The few voices of courage in a fearful crowd
then: When the people refused, {idea}two righteous men{/idea}, named by Ibn Abbas and others as Yusha' son of Nun and Kalib son of Yufna, urged them on. These men {idea}feared Allah{/idea}, and Allah had blessed them. Their advice: {reward}enter through the gate and you will win, and rely on Allah.{/reward}
now: A meeting where everyone agrees to cut a corner. A family gathering where everyone joins in gossip. {trap}Being the only voice feels impossible.{/trap} Two people were enough here. {idea}You can be one of them.{/idea}
old: If everyone else is afraid, I have no right to speak up.
new: Fear of Allah can make me one of the few who says: let us go forward.
try: Today, be the one who says the kind or honest thing in a group, even quietly.

title: You and your Lord go fight. We will sit here.
subtitle: When people want the result but send others to do it

row.title: never
sub: as long as they are there

then: Even after the two men spoke, the people refused again, more bluntly. {trap}Go, you and your Lord, and fight. We are staying right here.{/trap} They wanted the promised land, but {trap}wanted Musa and his Lord to win it for them.{/trap}
now: The group project where you let others do the work and put your name on it. The community fundraiser you share online but never give to. {trap}Watching from the couch.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks where your own effort is.{/idea}
old: Others are better at this. Let them handle it, and I will join later.
new: Leaving all the effort to others while I wait is the attitude this verse warns against.
try: Find one shared task at home or work you have been leaving to others. Do your part today.

title: I only have myself and my brother.
subtitle: A leader's honest prayer when people walk away

row.title: only myself
sub: and I bring it to Allah

then: After his people refused twice, Musa did not argue or force them. He turned to Allah: {idea}My Lord, I have power only over myself and my brother.{/idea} He asked to be {trap}separated from the people who openly disobeyed.{/trap}
now: You tried to keep the family together, to bring a friend back to prayer, to fix your team. {trap}They will not move.{/trap} Musa's words fit your mouth too: {idea}I only control myself.{/idea} Bring the rest to Allah.
old: If people around me do not change, I have failed.
new: I answer for myself, and I can bring the rest to Allah in prayer.
try: Make one honest dua tonight about someone you cannot change. Tell Allah you have done your part.

title: Forty years of wandering, and do not grieve.
subtitle: The cost of refusing the open gate

row.title: years of wandering
sub: lost, not sure where to go

then: Ibn Kathir says they were punished for forty years by being {trap}lost, wandering in the land, unsure where to go.{/trap} It was the result of refusing the command. Musa was told {idea}not to grieve{/idea} over people who had made their own choice.
now: Years of going in circles in the same job, the same habit, the same argument, {trap}because you said no to one hard step.{/trap} The wandering is not the end. {idea}Today's step can still be taken.{/idea}
old: Saying no to a hard step only costs me a little time.
new: Refusing the open gate can cost years, so I take the step while it is open.
try: Ask yourself which hard step you have been circling around. Write it down with a date.

title: Allah only accepts from those who are mindful of Him.
subtitle: Two brothers, two offerings, one envious heart
then: Ibn Kathir calls this {trap}the evil end of transgression, envy and injustice.{/trap} One brother's offering was accepted and the other's was not. Abu Ad-Darda' said that knowing Allah accepted {idea}even one prayer from me is better than this world and all in it{/idea}, because of this line.
now: Your colleague gets the promotion. Your sibling gets the praise. {trap}The thought arrives: why them and not me?{/trap} The verse turns you back to your own offering: {idea}is it done with a mindful heart?{/idea}
old: When someone else is blessed, something has been taken from me.
new: Their acceptance takes nothing from me. My work is to make my own offering sincere.
try: When envy comes today, make a short dua for that person's blessing to increase.

title: Even if you raise your hand, I will not raise mine.
subtitle: Strength held back by fear of Allah
then: Abdullah bin Amr said: {idea}by Allah, Habil was the stronger of the two, but fear of Allah held back his hand.{/idea} He refused to commit the same sin he was threatened with. Ibn Kathir says he chose {reward}patience and endurance.{/reward}
now: Someone insults you in the comments. A driver cuts you off and shouts. {trap}Your hand is already typing the reply.{/trap} The stronger son of Adam showed another kind of strength: {idea}I will not answer harm with the same harm.{/idea}
old: If I do not hit back, I look weak.
new: Holding back for Allah's sake is the stronger choice, not the weaker one.
try: The next time someone provokes you today, wait one full minute before responding, or do not respond.

title: The one who wrongs carries both burdens.
subtitle: The weight of a wrong falls on the one who does it
then: The brother who held back told the other that he would {trap}carry my sin and your sin.{/trap} Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and others said this means {trap}the sin of killing me, on top of your earlier sins.{/trap} He was warning his brother, still trying to stop him.
now: Someone spreads a lie about you at work. It feels like you are the one losing. {idea}But the weight of that wrong is on them, not on you.{/idea} Your job is to keep your own hands clean.
old: When someone wrongs me, I am the one who loses most.
new: A wrong lands heaviest on the one who commits it, so I keep my side clean.
try: Think of someone who wronged you. Leave the account with Allah and drop the replay in your head.

title: His own soul made the crime look reasonable.
subtitle: How the self talks a person into ruin
then: His brother had warned him, yet Ibn Kathir explains that {trap}his conscience encouraged him, making it seem like a sensible thing to do.{/trap} So he killed him and became {trap}one of the losers{/trap}, in this life and the next.
now: It is only a small lie. Everyone does it. They deserved it. {trap}The self is a skilled lawyer.{/trap} Before a wrong deed, it builds the argument. {idea}Notice when you start explaining to yourself why something wrong is fine.{/idea}
old: If I can explain it to myself, it must be okay.
new: My soul can make wrong look reasonable, so I check its arguments against Allah's guidance.
try: Catch one excuse you tell yourself today. Say it out loud and ask if it would hold before Allah.

title: A crow taught him what his own heart could not.
subtitle: Regret arrives after the deed, holding a shovel

row.title: his brother's body
sub: and no idea what to do

then: This closes the story of Adam's two sons. After the killing, Allah sent a crow scratching the ground to show him {idea}how to cover his brother's body.{/idea} He cried: {trap}woe to me, could I not even be like this crow?{/trap} He became one of the regretful.
now: The angry text you sent at midnight. The words you said to your mother in a fight. {trap}A minute later you are staring at what you did, not knowing how to fix it.{/trap} {idea}Regret is a sign to turn back, while turning back still helps.{/idea}
old: I will deal with the consequences later. Right now I just want to act.
new: Regret after a wrong comes fast and heavy, so I pause before the deed.
try: Before the next angry reply today, picture yourself one hour later. Then decide.

title: Save one life and it is as if you saved everyone.
subtitle: Why one human life weighs as much as all of humanity
then: Because of what Adam's son did, this rule was given. Ibn Kathir says it is so {idea}because there is no difference between one life and another.{/idea} Ibn Abbas explained that saving a life includes {reward}refusing to take a life Allah made sacred.{/reward} Then all people are safe from you.
now: You give blood once a year. You stop to help a stranger who collapsed on the platform. You talk a friend through the worst night of their life. {reward}By this verse, that is everyone.{/reward}
old: Helping one person barely makes a difference in a world this big.
new: One life saved carries the weight of all lives, because each one is sacred.
try: Do one thing today that protects a life: check on someone struggling, or sign up to donate blood.

title: Spreading terror on the land is among the gravest crimes.
subtitle: How seriously Allah treats people's safety
then: Right after the verse about one life, this verse names {trap}very severe penalties{/trap} for those who oppose Allah and spread corruption. Ibn Kathir says this includes {trap}blocking roads and spreading fear{/trap}. Mischief in the land, he says, covers many kinds of evil.
now: You are not a criminal. But you can still make a place feel unsafe: the office bully, the neighbor who scares children, the driver who terrorizes the road. {idea}The verse shows how much Allah values people feeling safe.{/idea}
old: Making people afraid is not a serious sin if no one gets hurt.
new: People's safety is so sacred to Allah that spreading fear is among the gravest wrongs.
try: Notice one place where people feel uneasy around you. Do one thing today to make them feel safe.

title: Even here, the door of return is open.
subtitle: Mercy right after the hardest verse
then: Directly after the most severe penalty, the verse opens an exception: {idea}those who return in repentance before they are caught.{/idea} It ends: {reward}know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.{/reward} Even at the edge, the door is shown.
now: You have a habit no one knows about yet. No one has caught you. {idea}This is the best time to stop: before anyone forces you.{/idea} The verse says turning back by choice is met with {reward}forgiveness and mercy.{/reward}
old: I will stop when I get caught or when things fall apart.
new: Coming back before anyone forces me is the return Allah honors.
try: Name one hidden habit you want to leave. Make a sincere intention today, before anything forces you.

title: Seek the means to come near Him.
subtitle: Mindfulness, a path toward Him, and steady effort
then: Ibn Abbas said wasilah means {idea}the means of approach.{/idea} Qatadah said: {idea}come near Him by obeying Him and doing what pleases Him.{/idea} Wasilah is also the highest rank in Paradise, and the Prophet ﷺ taught that whoever asks for it for him after the call to prayer {reward}will have his intercession.{/reward}
now: The adhan goes off on your phone. Usually you swipe it away. {idea}There is a short dua for that exact moment{/idea}, asking for the wasilah for the Prophet ﷺ. A thirty-second habit that brings you near.
old: Getting close to Allah needs something big that I am not ready for.
new: Every act that pleases Him is a step closer, even a short dua after the adhan.
try: After the next adhan, repeat its words and ask Allah to grant the Prophet ﷺ the wasilah.

title: The whole earth, twice over, would not buy a way out.
subtitle: On that Day, nothing works as ransom
then: Ibn Kathir cites a hadith: a man of the Fire is asked if he would ransom himself with the earth's fill of gold. He says yes. He is told: {trap}you lie, I asked you for less than that and you did not do it.{/trap} {idea}What was asked was small, and asked in time.{/idea}
now: You would give anything to undo a mistake once it is too late. Right now, {idea}what is asked of you is small{/idea}: a prayer, a kind word, a debt repaid. {trap}The price only grows when it is postponed.{/trap}
old: If I ever need to fix things with Allah, I will find a way then.
new: What He asks now is small, and later even the whole earth would not be enough.
try: Do one small act of obedience you have been delaying, today, while it is still small.

title: They will wish to leave, and there will be no exit.
subtitle: Why the time to leave the road is now
then: This verse follows the failed ransom of verse 36. Ibn Kathir explains that they will {trap}long to leave, but have no way of escaping.{/trap} The verse is stated plainly, so that {idea}the door is used while it is still open.{/idea}
now: You are not there. You are here, with a phone in your hand and a whole day ahead. {idea}Every exit from a wrong road is still open to you.{/idea} The verse is a mercy because it tells you this before the doors close.
old: Thinking about the end is depressing, so I avoid it.
new: Hearing about the end now is a mercy, because now I can still choose.
try: Ask Allah today, in your own words, to keep you far from the Fire and to make you leave every wrong road.

title: Taking what is not yours is a serious matter to Allah.
subtitle: A severe penalty, applied the same to everyone
then: Ibn Kathir notes that Islam set {idea}several conditions before this penalty could ever apply.{/idea} When a woman from a noble clan stole and people tried to intercede, the Prophet ﷺ said: those before you were destroyed because {trap}they excused the powerful and punished the weak.{/trap}
now: Office supplies taken home. A borrowed book never returned. The streaming account you were never meant to use. {trap}It feels too small to count.{/trap} {idea}This verse shows how serious Allah is about what belongs to others.{/idea}
old: Small things taken from big companies or rich people do not really count.
new: What belongs to others is a trust, and taking it matters to Allah, big or small.
try: Return one thing today that is not yours, or pay back something you owe, however small.

title: Repent and set things right, and He turns to you.
subtitle: No wrong is so heavy that the door closes

row.title: a clean start
sub: as on the day you were born

then: A woman who stole asked the Prophet ﷺ if she could still repent. He said: {reward}yes, today you are free of your sin as on the day your mother gave birth to you.{/reward} A'ishah said {idea}her repentance was sincere{/idea}, she married, and she used to visit her.
now: Your family still brings up what you did years ago. Your own mind replays it at night. {trap}You feel labeled for life.{/trap} The verse says {reward}Allah turns to the one who repents and reforms.{/reward} His view of you can be new today.
old: After what I did, I will always be that person.
new: Real repentance and a changed life can give me a clean start with Allah.
try: Turn one old regret into a quiet repentance today, and do one good deed that sets part of it right.

title: The heavens and the earth are His. So is the final word.
subtitle: Forgiveness and punishment rest with the Owner of all
then: This verse closes the passage on penalty and repentance. Ibn Kathir says Allah {idea}owns everything and decides what He wills, and no one can resist His judgment.{/idea} After the open door of verse 39, it reminds who {reward}holds the keys to forgiveness.{/reward}
now: People online have already judged you. Your old friends have made up their minds. {trap}Their verdict feels final.{/trap} {idea}It is not.{/idea} The only judgment that lasts belongs to the One who owns the heavens and the earth.
old: Once people have judged me, my case is closed.
new: Only Allah's judgment is final, and His forgiveness is in His hands, not theirs.
try: When someone's harsh opinion of you comes to mind today, turn it into a dua for Allah's forgiveness.

title: Take the answer only if it suits you.
subtitle: Shopping for a ruling, and words without hearts
then: The Prophet ﷺ is comforted: {idea}do not let them grieve you.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says some said we believe with their mouths while their hearts had no faith. Others came for a ruling and agreed among themselves: {trap}if he gives the easy answer, take it, and if not, refuse it.{/trap}
now: You ask three friends until one says what you wanted to hear. You search online until one video agrees with you. {trap}The answer was chosen before the question.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks if you are seeking truth or permission.{/idea}
old: I just want to hear one opinion that says I am fine.
new: Asking only to hear what suits me is not seeking guidance at all.
try: Think of one question you keep asking until you get the answer you like. Ask Allah for the truth instead.

title: If you judge, judge with justice. Allah loves the just.
subtitle: What you listen to and what you consume
then: The verse describes people who were {trap}eager listeners to falsehood and eager consumers of what is unlawful.{/trap} The Prophet ﷺ was told he could judge between them or turn away, and that if he judged, {idea}judge with justice, for Allah loves the just.{/idea}
now: The podcast full of rumors you keep playing. The side income you know is not clean. {trap}What you feed your ears and your stomach shapes you.{/trap} And when two friends ask you to settle a fight, {idea}be fair, even to the one you like less.{/idea}
old: What I listen to and where my money comes from is my own business.
new: What I take in shapes my heart, and fairness is owed even when I am the judge.
try: Unfollow or mute one source that mostly feeds you gossip or lies today.

title: Why ask, when you already hold the answer?
subtitle: Seeking judgment while turning from guidance you have
then: Ibn Kathir explains that these people came to the Prophet ﷺ for a ruling, though {idea}they had Allah's judgment in their own scripture.{/idea} The question in the verse is gentle and sharp: how? And then {trap}they turned away even after that.{/trap}
now: You ask your friend whether you should apologize to your mother. You already know. You ask the imam about that deal at work. {trap}You already know.{/trap} {idea}Often the problem is not knowledge but willingness.{/idea}
old: I am not sure what is right. I need more opinions.
new: Most of the time I already know what is right. The step is following it.
try: Pick one thing you already know you should do and have been asking about. Do it instead of asking.

title: Fear Me, not people, and do not sell My verses cheaply.
subtitle: Guarding revelation when it costs you
then: The verse honors the Torah: {reward}guidance and light{/reward}, by which prophets and scholars judged, because {idea}they were entrusted with Allah's Book.{/idea} The warning to everyone who carries a scripture: {trap}do not fear people, and do not exchange My verses for a small price.{/trap}
now: Your manager wants you to sign off on something dishonest. Your friends laugh at something you know is wrong. {trap}Staying quiet keeps the job and the friends.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks whose reaction you fear more.{/idea}
old: A little silence about the truth is the price of getting along.
new: Trading what Allah said for people's approval is a very cheap sale.
try: In one small moment today, say the honest thing gently, even if it costs you a little approval.

title: Justice is equal. Forgiving it is charity.
subtitle: A right given, and the reward of letting it go

row.title: equal justice
sub: harm for harm, same for all

key.label: What you can do with a right

then: Ibn Kathir says the law was meant to {idea}treat everyone equally and fairly.{/idea} Then the verse opens a door: whoever gives up the right as charity, it is expiation. The Prophet ﷺ said that whoever forgives a wound done to him, {reward}Allah will pardon him something similar.{/reward}
now: Your cousin damaged your car and never paid. Your coworker embarrassed you in front of everyone. {idea}You have every right to demand it back.{/idea} The verse does not cancel your right. It shows you {reward}a better use for it.{/reward}
old: If I let it go, I am letting them win.
new: My right is real, and giving it up for Allah becomes charity that covers my own faults.
try: Forgive one small debt or wrong someone owes you today, and tell Allah you did it for Him.

title: Isa came confirming what came before him.
subtitle: One chain of guidance and light
then: Ibn Kathir says Isa {idea}believed in the Torah and ruled by it.{/idea} The Gospel he received was {reward}a guidance that directs to the truth and a light that removes doubts{/reward}, and an admonition for those mindful of Allah.
now: You may think of faith as something that started with you or your family. {idea}It is part of a long chain of messengers{/idea}, each confirming the last. Every time you pray, you join a line much older than you.
old: Each messenger came with a completely separate message.
new: The messengers came in one line, confirming each other, all pointing to the same Lord.
try: Read about one earlier prophet today and notice what his message shares with the Quran.

title: Live by what you say you believe.
subtitle: Holding a book is not the same as following it
then: Ibn Kathir explains that this means {idea}to believe in all that is in it and follow all its commands{/idea}, including its good news of a coming messenger. Those who did not were called {trap}rebellious, preferring falsehood and abandoning truth.{/trap}
now: The Quran sits on your shelf in a nice cover. You know its words are true. {trap}But how much of your week is shaped by it?{/trap} The verse addresses one people, but {idea}the question fits every person who holds a book from Allah.{/idea}
old: Having the Quran at home and believing in it is enough.
new: A book from Allah is meant to shape my decisions, not just sit on my shelf.
try: Choose one verse you know well and let it guide one decision you make today.

title: He could have made you one. Instead: race to do good.
subtitle: The Quran as guardian, and differences as a test
then: Ibn Abbas said muhaymin means {idea}trustworthy, a witness, and guardian{/idea} over the earlier books. The verse says Allah could have made everyone one community, but chose {trap}to test you with what He gave you.{/trap} So {reward}race to good.{/reward} He will explain the differences on return.
now: The comment section where everyone argues about religion. The family dinner that turns into a debate. {trap}Hours spent proving you are right.{/trap} {idea}The verse says: spend that energy racing to do good, and leave the final word to Allah.{/idea}
old: Winning the argument is the most important thing.
new: Differences are a test, and my answer is to race in good deeds while Allah settles the rest.
try: Skip one argument today, online or at home, and spend that time doing a good deed instead.

title: Beware of being pulled away from part of the guidance.
subtitle: Pressure to drop some of what Allah revealed
then: Even the Prophet ﷺ is told: {trap}beware lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah revealed.{/trap} Ibn Kathir says this means not following {idea}the ideas people promote{/idea} that turn them from revelation. The danger is not all at once, but {trap}some of it.{/trap}
now: Friends at work say: just skip the prayer for this meeting. Others say: everyone bends the truth a little on these forms. {trap}Each time it is only a small part.{/trap} {idea}Notice how much gets dropped one small part at a time.{/idea}
old: Giving up one small part to fit in does not really change anything.
new: Guidance is lost a piece at a time, so I hold on to each piece.
try: Pick one practice you have quietly dropped to fit in. Bring it back today, calmly.

title: Who judges better than Allah, for those who are certain?
subtitle: Old customs versus guidance
then: This verse closes the passage on judging by revelation. The question points back to {trap}the judgment of the time of ignorance{/trap}, the customs before guidance came. Then: {idea}who is better than Allah in judgment, for a people who are certain?{/idea}
now: The family feud nobody remembers the reason for, kept alive for years. The tradition of a wedding that leaves a young couple in debt. {trap}Because that is how we have always done it.{/trap} {idea}Certainty in Allah lets you question the custom.{/idea}
old: Our customs are part of who we are, so they must be right.
new: When a custom and Allah's guidance differ, His judgment is the better one.
try: Name one custom in your family or culture that you have never checked against the Quran. Look into it.

title: Your deepest loyalty shapes who you become.
subtitle: Allegiance in a time of open hostility

row.title: it shapes me
sub: I become like those I side with

then: This verse came when the young community in Madinah faced open hostility. Ibn Kathir describes people with {trap}a disease of doubt and hesitation{/trap} who rushed to secret alliances with the other side, {trap}afraid of what might happen.{/trap} The verse says loyalty is not neutral: {idea}you become one of those you side with.{/idea}
now: The group at work that cuts corners, and you join so you are safe when layoffs come. The friends whose values you do not share, but whose approval you cannot lose. {idea}The verse is about your own heart: who do you really stand with?{/idea}
old: Where my loyalty lies is just a practical choice. It does not change me.
new: The ones I give my deepest loyalty to slowly shape who I become.
try: Ask yourself honestly: whose approval do I fear losing most? Bring that answer to Allah in dua.

title: Hedging your bets, just in case. Then regret.
subtitle: A foot in both camps out of fear
then: Ibn Kathir explains that some excused their secret alliances by saying {trap}we fear a misfortune may hit us.{/trap} They wanted favor with the other side in case the believers lost. The verse answers: {idea}perhaps Allah will bring victory or a decision.{/idea} Then {trap}they regretted what they had hidden.{/trap}
now: You keep the shady contact on speed dial, just in case. You say yes to both sides in a family fight so no one is angry. {trap}Fear writes the plan.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks you to trust that Allah's decision is coming.{/idea}
old: It is smart to keep a foot in every camp, just in case.
new: Hedging out of fear leads to regret. Trusting Allah's decision leads to peace.
try: Notice one backup plan you keep out of fear rather than wisdom. Ask Allah to replace that fear with trust.

title: They swore their strongest oaths, and it all fell apart.
subtitle: When words and allegiance are finally compared
then: Ibn Kathir says when the signs came together, the truth became clear to the believers, who were {trap}amazed at those who swore their faithfulness while their claims were lies.{/trap} {trap}All that they did was in vain.{/trap} Oaths did not hide what was in their hearts.
now: I am always here for you, you tell your friend, then you vanish when they need help moving. I am loyal to this company, until a better offer comes. {idea}The verse asks you to make your words and your stand match.{/idea}
old: Saying the right words is enough to show I am loyal.
new: My loyalty is shown by where I stand when it matters, not by how strongly I swear.
try: Think of one person you told I am with you. Show it with one action today.

title: A people He loves, and who love Him.
subtitle: Gentle with their own, unafraid of blame

row.title: Allah's favor
sub: He gives it to whom He wills

then: Ibn Kathir calls these the qualities of {idea}complete believers{/idea}. Abu Dharr said the Prophet ﷺ told him to love the poor, keep ties with relatives even if they cut him, and {idea}say the truth even if it is bitter, not fearing anyone's blame for Allah.{/idea} The verse says {reward}this is Allah's favor.{/reward}
now: You are harsh with your own family and soft with strangers who might judge you. {trap}You change your words when someone might laugh.{/trap} The verse flips it: {idea}gentle with your own people, steady in the truth, free from the fear of blame.{/idea}
old: Avoiding criticism is more important than saying what is right.
new: The people Allah loves are gentle with their own and do not fear blame for His sake.
try: Call one relative who has not called you in a long time. Be gentle, ask nothing.

title: Your true ally: Allah, His Messenger, and those who pray.
subtitle: The circle of real support
then: After warning against misplaced loyalty, the verse names the true circle. Ibn Kathir says these are believers who {idea}establish prayer, give what is owed to the needy{/idea}, and {reward}attend prayer together in the mosques and spend in charity.{/reward}
now: When your father was in hospital, who came? When you lost your job, who sent food? {idea}Often the people at the mosque, the friend who prays, the neighbor who gives quietly.{/idea} The verse says: these are your allies. Stay close to them.
old: My real support comes from people with influence and money.
new: My real allies are Allah, His Messenger ﷺ, and the people who pray and give.
try: Pray one prayer today in congregation, and greet one person there by name.

title: Those on Allah's side are the ones who prevail.
subtitle: The party of Allah, in the end

row.title: victorious
sub: in this life and the next

then: This verse completes verse 55. Ibn Kathir says that those who accept the allegiance of {idea}Allah, His Messenger and the believers{/idea} will {reward}gain success in this life and the Hereafter.{/reward} The side that wins is not the loudest one, but the one with Allah.
now: You feel outnumbered: the only one fasting at the office, the only one who left the bad deal. {trap}It looks like you are on the losing side.{/trap} {idea}The verse says the side with Allah prevails, even if it takes time.{/idea}
old: I should join whichever side looks like it is winning.
new: Being with Allah is the winning side, even when I feel alone.
try: Do one right thing today that leaves you in the minority, and do it calmly.

title: Do not take as close friends those who mock your faith.
subtitle: Guarding your heart from ridicule
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the verse concerns those who {trap}made the best acts of worship a subject of jest and play.{/trap} It ends: {idea}fear Allah, if you are truly believers.{/idea} The issue is not difference. It is taking as close allies those who {trap}make a joke of what you hold sacred.{/trap}
now: The friend who laughs every time you step out to pray. The group chat that turns your fasting into a meme. {trap}You laugh along to fit in.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks who you let into the inner circle of your heart.{/idea}
old: If I want to keep friends, I need to laugh along when they mock religion.
new: I can be kind to everyone and still keep my inner circle for those who respect my faith.
try: Next time someone jokes about your faith, do not laugh along. Smile, stay calm, and change the subject.

title: The call to prayer, the best call there is.
subtitle: How you treat the adhan says something

row.title: ridicule
sub: from those who do not reason

then: Az-Zuhri said: {idea}Allah mentioned the adhan in His Book{/idea}, in this verse. Ibn Kathir calls the call to prayer {reward}the best action there is, for those with sound minds.{/reward} The Prophet ﷺ said that when the adhan is called, {trap}Shaytan runs away so he will not hear it.{/trap}
now: The adhan app goes off in the middle of a meeting and you silence it, a little embarrassed. {trap}You treat it like noise.{/trap} The verse warns about mocking it. {idea}Ask yourself how you answer it.{/idea}
old: The adhan is just a reminder I can snooze.
new: The adhan is the best call I will hear today, and how I answer it matters.
try: At the next adhan, stop what you are doing and repeat its words quietly until it ends.

title: Is our only fault that we believe?
subtitle: Make sure faith is the only thing they can blame

row.title: we believe
sub: in Allah and all He revealed

key.label: What they can blame you for

then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to ask: do you criticize us only because {idea}we believe in Allah, in what was sent to us and what was sent before?{/idea} Ibn Kathir notes that this is {reward}no cause of blame at all.{/reward} He compares it with believers in another surah whose only fault was their faith.
now: Your coworker rolls their eyes when you mention you are fasting. Fine. But if they also see you late, rude and gossiping, {trap}they will blame your faith for your faults.{/trap} {idea}Let your faith be the only thing anyone can criticize.{/idea}
old: If people dislike me, it must be because of my religion.
new: I should make sure my faith is the only thing they can point to, not my behavior.
try: Do one thing today that shows good character to someone who does not share your faith.

title: What truly lowers a person is serving false masters.
subtitle: Who is worse in rank, in Allah's measure
then: This answers the mockery of verse 59. The verse lists those who {trap}earned Allah's curse and anger{/trap}, and those who {trap}served Taghut{/trap}, false masters obeyed instead of Allah. Ibn Kathir says the point is: how can anyone mock {idea}a faith built on worshipping Allah alone?{/idea}
now: The phone that decides when you sleep. The money you chase until it owns you. The opinion of people you obey over Allah. {trap}Masters can be quiet.{/trap} {idea}The verse asks which of them you are serving today.{/idea}
old: What makes a person low is what others say about them.
new: What truly lowers a person is serving anything in place of Allah.
try: Name one thing that controls your day more than it should. Take one hour back from it for Allah today.

title: They walked in with it and walked out with it.
subtitle: Sitting near guidance without letting it in
then: In Madinah some people came to sit with the Prophet ﷺ and said all the right words. Ibn Kathir explains that they {trap}entered with disbelief hidden in their hearts and left with it{/trap}, so the knowledge and advice they heard did nothing for them. {idea}Allah knew what they were hiding.{/idea}
now: Friday khutbah. You are on the carpet, phone face down, nodding. Twenty minutes later you are in the car and cannot remember one sentence. You came in with your worries and your habits, and you {trap}left with exactly the same ones{/trap}. {idea}Being in the room is not the same as letting it in.{/idea}
old: If I show up to the reminder, I have done my part.
new: The question is what I walk out with, and only Allah sees that.
try: After the next talk or lecture you hear, write down one sentence from it and one thing you will change.

title: Racing toward the wrong thing.
subtitle: The speed people show for sin and easy money
then: The verse describes many people of that time who were {trap}hurrying into sin and transgression{/trap}. Ibn Kathir says this meant wronging others and consuming their wealth unjustly, through bribes and interest. The verse calls it plainly: {trap}evil is what they were doing.{/trap}
now: The side deal at work that skips the paperwork. The cash that needs no receipt. You did not stumble into it. You {trap}moved fast before you could think twice{/trap}. Watch your own speed. {idea}Hurry is often the sign that a part of you already knows.{/idea}
old: Everyone grabs what they can, I am just quicker.
new: When I rush toward money or a wrong, the rush itself is a warning.
try: Next time you feel in a hurry to say yes to a deal or a reply, wait one hour first.

title: Why did the ones who knew stay quiet?
subtitle: The silence of people who should speak
then: The verse turns from the wrongdoers to the learned men who watched and said nothing. Ibn Kathir notes that the blame here falls on the scholars, because {trap}they gave up forbidding evil{/trap}. Ibn 'Abbas said there is {idea}no verse in the Quran with a more severe warning{/idea} than this one.
now: The family group chat. Someone forwards a cruel rumour about a cousin. You know it is false. You are the one people listen to. You {trap}leave it on read{/trap} and hope it goes away. {idea}Knowing and staying silent has a weight of its own.{/idea}
old: If I am not doing the wrong, I am not part of it.
new: If I could have spoken kindly and did not, my silence is something I did.
try: Think of one place where your voice is trusted. Next time something wrong passes there, say one gentle sentence.

title: His hands are open wide, always giving.
subtitle: Answering the thought that Allah holds back
then: Some people of that time spoke of Allah as stingy. Ibn 'Abbas explained they did not mean a literal hand, but that {trap}He does not spend from what He has{/trap}. The verse answers: {idea}both His hands are outstretched.{/idea} The Prophet ﷺ said Allah's right hand is full and no spending decreases it, and that Allah says: {reward}Spend, and I will spend on you.{/reward}
now: Payday is late again. The rent reminder lights up your phone. A quiet thought slides in: Allah has forgotten me, He gives to everyone else. That thought is {trap}a tied hand pictured on the Giver{/trap}. Count what reached you this week without asking. {reward}It came from the same open hands.{/reward}
old: When money is tight, it feels like Allah is holding back from me.
new: His hands are open. What He gives and when is wisdom, not shortage.
try: Today, give something small to someone, even a little, as a way of trusting the open hand.

title: If only they had believed, the slate was ready.
subtitle: The door that stayed open the whole time
then: Right after the hard words about what some People of the Scripture had said and done, the verse does not close the door. It says {idea}if only they had believed and been mindful of Allah{/idea}, He would have {reward}removed their misdeeds and admitted them to Gardens of Pleasure.{/reward}
now: Late at night, scrolling back through your own history in your head. The things you said, the years you drifted. You decide {trap}it is too late for someone like you.{/trap} This verse comes straight after a long list of wrongs and still says: {reward}if only.{/reward} The door was open the whole time.
old: After what I have done, I am past the point of being forgiven.
new: Even after a long list of wrongs, Allah's offer is still on the table.
try: Tonight, before sleeping, ask Allah sincerely to forgive one specific thing, by name.

title: Live the Book and provision rains from every side.
subtitle: Obedience opens doors above and below
then: The verse speaks of those given earlier scripture: had they truly {idea}upheld what was revealed to them{/idea}, they would have eaten {reward}from above them and from beneath their feet.{/reward} Then it is careful: among them is {idea}a moderate community{/idea}, while many do evil.
now: Two things to take home. First, your own: the Quran on the shelf, wrapped and dusted, versus the Quran lived in how you earn and speak. Second, how you talk about people: the verse that criticises still says {idea}not all of them{/idea}. When you catch yourself saying {trap}they are all like that{/trap}, about anyone, stop.
old: Provision is just about how hard I work and how lucky I get.
new: Living by what Allah sent opens provision, and fairness means never painting everyone one colour.
try: Pick one habit in how you earn or spend and bring it closer to what the Quran asks, starting today.

title: Deliver all of it. Allah will guard you.
subtitle: The Messenger's charge, and the promise of protection
then: 'A'ishah said that whoever claims the Prophet ﷺ hid any part of the revelation is lying. Before this verse, he was guarded at night. When it came, {reward}he told the guards to go, for Allah would protect him.{/reward} At the Farewell Hajj he asked the crowd, and they testified {idea}he had conveyed the message{/idea}, and he said: O Allah, bear witness.
now: There is something true you need to say to a family member: a debt, a habit, a hard honest word. You keep holding it back, afraid of the reaction. And when you do say it, you want them to change on the spot. {idea}Your part is to say it well. The result is not yours to carry.{/idea}
old: If they do not change after I speak, I have failed.
new: My job is to convey honestly and kindly. Guidance belongs to Allah.
try: Say one true thing you have been holding back, gently, and then leave the result with Allah.

title: Holding a book is not standing on it.
subtitle: Having scripture versus living by it

picture.label: Two ways to have a book

row.title: the label
sub: I belong, so I am fine

then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to say that holding scripture means {trap}standing on nothing{/trap} until it is truly upheld. He is also told: {idea}do not grieve over those who refuse.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains this as: do not be sad or shaken by their rejection.
now: You have the app on your phone, the framed verse in the hallway, the Muslim name on your ID. Then you ask what you actually did with the Book this week. A label is {trap}ground that is not there{/trap} until you walk on it. And when people you love turn away, {idea}you are allowed to let the sadness go.{/idea}
old: Being a Muslim on paper is my firm ground.
new: I only have ground under me when I live what I say I believe.
try: Choose one verse you know by heart and do one thing today that it asks.

title: Faith, the Last Day, good deeds: then no fear.
subtitle: What actually removes fear and grief
then: The verse lists groups by name, then says what matters: {idea}belief in Allah and the Last Day, and righteous action.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains that after the Prophet ﷺ was sent, righteous action means following what he brought. For those who hold this, {reward}there is no fear of what is coming and no grief over what is lost.{/reward}
now: Hospital corridor, waiting for a result. Fear about tomorrow, grief about what you already lost. Your name, your family, your community cannot quiet that. The verse names what does: {idea}real belief in Allah and the Day, shown in what you do.{/idea}
old: Belonging to the right community is what keeps me safe.
new: What calms fear and grief is real faith in Allah and the Day, carried into action.
try: Do one quiet good deed today that no one will know about, for the Last Day only.

title: They kept the parts that suited them.
subtitle: When guidance clashes with what we want
then: Allah reminds that He took a covenant from the Children of Israel and sent them messengers. Ibn Kathir explains that {trap}whatever part of the law agreed with their desires, they took; the rest they left.{/trap} When a messenger brought what they disliked, some denied him and some killed him.
now: A friend tells you, kindly, that the way you speak to your mother is harsh. Last week you loved her advice about your career. This week you {trap}decide she does not understand you{/trap}. Notice the filter: {idea}you accept guidance until it costs you something.{/idea}
old: I take the advice that makes sense to me and ignore the rest.
new: Guidance that goes against my wants is often the part I need most.
try: Think of one piece of advice you brushed off because it stung. Give it one honest minute today.

title: They assumed nothing would follow, so they stopped seeing.
subtitle: How feeling safe from consequences dulls the heart
then: Ibn Kathir explains that they {trap}thought there would be no trial or repercussion{/trap} for the wrongs they did, so they became blind and deaf to the truth. Then {reward}Allah turned to them in forgiveness{/reward}, and many of them went back to the same blindness. The verse ends: Allah sees what they do.
now: The first time you skipped a prayer, it felt heavy. Nothing happened. The second time, lighter. A year later you do not notice anymore. That quiet slide is {trap}the eyes closing slowly{/trap}. And the mercy is that the door reopens, again and again. {idea}Walk through it and keep your eyes open this time.{/idea}
old: Nothing bad happened, so it must not matter much.
new: Getting away with something can be the very thing that blinds me.
try: Name one wrong you have stopped feeling bad about. Ask Allah to make you feel it again.

title: The Messiah himself said: worship Allah, my Lord and yours.
subtitle: A messenger pointing away from himself
then: Ibn Kathir notes that the first words of 'Isa, even as a baby in the cradle, were {idea}I am a servant of Allah.{/idea} As a grown prophet he told the Children of Israel: {idea}worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.{/idea} The verse then states soberly that {trap}setting up partners with Allah closes Paradise{/trap}, and the wrongdoers have no helpers.
now: A good teacher, a beloved sheikh, a parent you admire. Real love can slide into something else: you check what they would say before you check what Allah said. The best of them would say what the Messiah said: {idea}worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord.{/idea} Honour them by following where they point.
old: The closer I feel to a righteous person, the closer I am to Allah.
new: The righteous point away from themselves, toward Allah alone.
try: Think of someone whose words you treat as final. Today, look up what Allah says on one thing they taught.

title: There is no god except One God.
subtitle: The line the whole surah keeps returning to
then: The verse answers a belief that made Allah one of three. As-Suddi linked it to {trap}taking 'Isa and his mother as gods beside Allah{/trap}, as the end of this surah also describes. The reply is short: {idea}there is no god but One God.{/idea} The warning is tied to a condition: if they do not stop.
now: Your heart can split its trust three ways without saying a word: Allah, your salary, and your own cleverness. When the job wobbles, everything wobbles. {idea}One God{/idea} means one place your heart finally rests. Everything else is a gift from Him, {trap}not a second pillar beside Him.{/trap}
old: I trust Allah, plus my income, plus my plans, equally.
new: Only One is God. My plans and income are tools He gave me.
try: Before checking your bank app today, say: my provision is from Allah alone.

title: Even then: will they not turn back to Him?
subtitle: An invitation after the gravest claim
then: Right after the heaviest warning, the very next verse asks a gentle question: {idea}will they not repent and seek His forgiveness?{/idea} Ibn Kathir calls this a sign of {reward}Allah's generosity, kindness and mercy{/reward}: even after so grave a claim, He calls them to return so He can forgive.
now: You have written someone off. A relative who did something unforgivable, a friend who wandered far. Or you have written yourself off. The Quran, straight after its sternest words, {reward}asks the door-question{/reward}. If Allah keeps the invitation open, {idea}you can stop closing it in your head.{/idea}
old: Some people, maybe me, are simply too far gone.
new: Allah calls even the gravest wrongdoers back. No one is outside the invitation.
try: Make one dua today for a person you had quietly given up on.

title: They both ate food.
subtitle: Honoured servants, not gods
then: The verse gives a calm, simple proof. 'Isa was {idea}a messenger like many before him{/idea}. His mother was a siddiqah, a woman of complete truthful faith. Ibn Kathir explains the point of {idea}they both used to eat food{/idea}: they needed nourishment like every servant of Allah, so they were servants, not gods.
now: Hunger at 4pm in Ramadan. You feel how much you need: water, food, sleep, air. That need is not a weakness to hide. {idea}It is the plain mark of being created.{/idea} The greatest people who ever lived carried that same mark, and it made them honoured servants, {trap}not less.{/trap}
old: Truly great people must be somehow beyond ordinary needs.
new: Even the greatest of people needed food. Needing is what servants do, and only Allah needs nothing.
try: At your next meal, pause before the first bite and thank Allah for meeting a need you cannot meet alone.

title: Why turn to what cannot help or harm you?
subtitle: The One who hears and knows
then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to ask a direct question. Ibn Kathir explains it: how can anyone worship things that {trap}cannot prevent harm or bring benefit{/trap}, that do not hear, see or know, {idea}instead of Allah, who hears what His servants say and knows all things?{/idea}
now: The lucky charm in the car. The horoscope app you open "just for fun" before an interview. The person whose approval you check like a weather report. None of them {trap}heard you this morning{/trap}. {idea}Allah heard every word, even the ones you did not say.{/idea}
old: A little extra luck or reassurance on the side cannot hurt.
new: Only Allah hears me and can help me. Everything else hears nothing.
try: Remove one thing you keep for luck or reassurance, and ask Allah directly instead.

title: Do not go past the truth in your religion.
subtitle: Exaggeration, even in love, leads astray
then: Ibn Kathir explains the warning as: {trap}do not exaggerate in praising the one you were told to honour.{/trap} They raised a prophet to the rank of a god, because they followed teachers before them who {trap}went astray and misled many{/trap}. The fix is to stay {idea}within the truth{/idea}.
now: The online preacher you follow, whose every clip you share without checking. The relative who makes the religion so strict that the young people in the family quietly leave. Both {trap}add to the truth out of zeal{/trap}. {idea}Love for the deen means keeping it the size Allah made it.{/idea}
old: Going further than required can only be a good thing.
new: Going past the truth, even out of love, is still leaving the truth.
try: Before you share a religious clip today, check what the source is and whether it adds to what is known.

title: Their own prophets named the problem: constant disobedience.
subtitle: Why a curse came through Dawud and 'Isa
then: Allah says that those who disbelieved among the Children of Israel were cursed {idea}on the tongue of their own prophets, Dawud and 'Isa{/idea}. The verse states the reason clearly: {trap}they disobeyed and kept transgressing.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains: disobeying Allah and wronging His creatures.
now: You hear a warning and think of other people. But the reason given is a behaviour, and behaviours travel. {trap}The small disobedience you repeat every day{/trap} is the same seed. The verse is a mirror: {idea}what you keep doing is what defines you.{/idea}
old: Warnings like this are about other people, not me.
new: The reason was a habit of disobedience, and that can grow in anyone, including me.
try: Pick one small sin you repeat daily. Skip it just for today.

title: No one told anyone to stop.
subtitle: A community where wrong goes unchallenged
then: Their habit was that {trap}they did not forbid one another from the wrong they did.{/trap} Ibn Kathir quotes the Prophet ﷺ: whoever sees a wrong should {idea}change it with his hand, then his tongue, then at least his heart{/idea}. He also quotes: fear of people should not stop you saying the truth you know, and that no one is asked to take on trials beyond what they can bear.
now: Your office jokes about a colleague who is not in the room. Everyone laughs a little. You can change the subject, say "not cool", or at least not laugh. {idea}Each of those counts.{/idea} The only option that does not is {trap}joining in because everyone else is.{/trap}
old: Speaking up is someone else's job, I would only make it awkward.
new: There is always some level I can act at, even if it is only in my heart.
try: Next time a cruel joke starts, change the subject or simply do not laugh.

title: What you send ahead by the side you take.
subtitle: Loyalty given to those who oppose the truth
then: Mujahid said this verse refers to the hypocrites. Ibn Kathir explains that by {trap}giving their loyalty to those who rejected faith instead of the believers{/trap}, they sent ahead an evil deed for themselves. It planted hypocrisy in their hearts and {trap}brought Allah's anger.{/trap}
now: At work there is a crowd that mocks anything to do with faith. To fit in, you laugh along, hide your prayer, roll your eyes when they do. Then you start {trap}defending them against the people who care about you{/trap}. Whose side you take is {idea}something you are sending ahead of yourself.{/idea}
old: Who I side with socially is just a matter of convenience.
new: The side I take is a deed I send ahead, and it shapes my heart.
try: Do one small thing today that shows openly which values you stand with, kindly.

title: Real faith would have chosen different friends.
subtitle: Belief shows in whom you lean on
then: The verse explains the root. Ibn Kathir: {idea}had they sincerely believed in Allah, His Messenger and the Quran{/idea}, they would not have secretly supported those against the believers. But {trap}many of them were defiant{/trap}. Their friendships exposed what their words hid.
now: Scroll through the five people you message most. The ones whose opinions you repeat. The ones you go to when things fall apart. {idea}That list says something about your faith{/idea} that a status update cannot. It is never too late to {reward}add someone good to it.{/reward}
old: My faith is between me and Allah, my friends are a separate matter.
new: The people I lean on reveal what I truly believe.
try: Message one person who helps you be better and arrange to see them this week.

title: Hearts without arrogance came closest.
subtitle: Why humility drew people near to the believers
then: Sa'id bin Jubayr, As-Suddi and others said these verses came about a delegation sent by An-Najashi, king of Abyssinia, to hear the Prophet ﷺ. The verse contrasts the hostility the believers met then with the warmth of others, and gives the reason for that warmth: {idea}knowledge, worship, and that they were not arrogant.{/idea} Ibn Kathir names {trap}defiance and belittling others{/trap} as what hardens hearts.
now: Think of the last time someone corrected you in front of others. Did you listen, or did your pride rise first? The verse does not measure people by labels. It measures {idea}the softness of a heart toward truth.{/idea} Ask which way {trap}your own pride{/trap} pulls you.
old: Who is close to the truth depends on which group they belong to.
new: Humility brings a heart near to the truth. Arrogance pushes it away, in anyone.
try: Today, when someone points out a mistake you made, say thank you before anything else.

title: They heard it, recognised it, and their eyes overflowed.
subtitle: Tears that come from recognising the truth
then: Ibn Kathir reports that when the delegation heard the Prophet ﷺ recite, {reward}they embraced Islam, cried and were humbled.{/reward} Qatadah said they were followers of 'Isa who, on hearing the Quran, {idea}believed without hesitation{/idea}. They asked Allah to write them among the witnesses to the truth.
now: You have heard the same surah a hundred times in taraweeh. Your mind drifts to the car park. Then one night one verse lands, and your throat tightens. {reward}That tightening is a gift.{/reward} Do not rush past it or wipe it away in embarrassment. {idea}Let the truth reach you.{/idea}
old: Crying when I hear the Quran is a little embarrassing.
new: Tears from recognising the truth are a sign of a living heart.
try: Listen tonight to one short passage of Quran with its meaning, slowly, with no phone in hand.

title: Why should we not believe?
subtitle: When the truth arrives, the only question left
then: The delegation's words continue: {idea}why should we not believe in Allah and the truth that has come to us?{/idea} They hoped their Lord would {reward}admit them with the righteous{/reward}. Ibn Kathir describes them as people who follow the truth wherever and whenever they find it.
now: You know you should start praying on time, or call your father, or stop that one habit. You keep asking: why should I, right now? Flip it. {idea}Why should I not?{/idea} Most of the reasons you find are {trap}just delays dressed up as thinking.{/trap}
old: I will change once I am fully convinced and ready.
new: When the truth is clear, the honest question is what is stopping me.
try: Pick one good change you keep postponing. Ask yourself, why not today, and do the first step.

title: Rewarded for what they said, from the heart.
subtitle: Sincere words of faith answered with Gardens

row.title: the doers of good
sub: who follow the truth they find

then: Allah rewarded them {idea}for what they said{/idea}: their sincere declaration of faith. The reward is {reward}Gardens beneath which rivers flow, where they remain forever.{/reward} Ibn Kathir says this is the reward of those who follow and obey the truth wherever they find it.
now: Your words count. The quiet "I believe, ya Allah" in a hospital waiting room, the shahadah you said as a child and again as an adult, meaning it this time. Allah {reward}honours sincere words{/reward}. {idea}Say them like you mean them, and then live like you said them.{/idea}
old: Words are cheap, only big deeds matter.
new: Sincere words of faith are themselves honoured by Allah.
try: Say your shahadah slowly today, thinking about each word.

title: The other path, stated plainly.
subtitle: Rejecting the signs and where it leads
then: Right after the reward of the humble listeners, the verse gives the contrast in one line. Ibn Kathir explains: those who {trap}disbelieved, denied and opposed{/trap} the signs are the people of the Fire. The same recitation was heard by both. {idea}The response made the difference.{/idea}
now: Two people sit in the same talk. One leaves softened, one leaves annoyed. You are both of those people on different days. The question is not whether you heard the truth. {idea}It is what you do in the minute after.{/idea} Push away from {trap}the reflex to dismiss.{/trap}
old: Hearing the truth is enough to be safe.
new: Hearing is the same for everyone. Accepting or denying is what decides.
try: Next time a reminder irritates you, pause and ask what in it might be true for you.

title: Do not forbid yourself the good Allah allowed.
subtitle: Against making religion harder than He made it

row.title: no bed
sub: I will never sleep on one

row.title: the Sunnah
sub: fast and eat, pray and sleep

then: Some Companions wanted to give up meat, marriage and sleep to be more devout. The Prophet ﷺ said: {idea}I fast and break my fast, I pray and I sleep, I eat meat and I marry. Whoever turns from my way is not of me.{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains the balance: {trap}neither banning the lawful nor indulging to excess.{/trap}
now: A burst of guilt after a lazy week, and suddenly you plan to wake at 3am every night, fast every day and quit everything fun. By Thursday you have quit the plan instead. {trap}Harshness on yourself is not the Sunnah.{/trap} {idea}The middle way is the one you can keep.{/idea}
old: The harder I am on myself, the more pious I am.
new: The Prophet ﷺ ate, slept and married. Balance is the path, not a compromise.
try: Replace one unrealistic religious goal with a small one you can keep every day this week.

title: Eat the good that He gave, and stay mindful.
subtitle: Enjoyment and taqwa at the same table
then: After telling the believers not to ban what is lawful, the next verse invites them: {reward}eat of what Allah has provided, lawful and good.{/reward} Ibn Kathir adds the second half: {idea}have taqwa of Allah in all your affairs{/idea}, obeying Him and seeking His pleasure.
now: Sunday lunch at your aunt's. The rice, the chicken, the laughter. You do not need to feel guilty for enjoying it. {reward}It is His provision.{/reward} Taqwa here looks like a bismillah before, an alhamdulillah after, {idea}and leftovers sent to the neighbour.{/idea}
old: Really enjoying food feels a bit unspiritual.
new: Enjoying lawful food with awareness of Allah is itself part of faith.
try: At your next meal, eat slowly, say bismillah aloud, and thank Allah at the end.

title: Guard your oaths.
subtitle: Words sworn by Allah carry weight

row.title: slips of the tongue
sub: no, by Allah, said by habit

then: Ibn Kathir explains that Allah does not hold people to {idea}unintended oaths{/idea}, like a habitual "no, by Allah" in speech. Deliberate oaths are different. The verse lays out a repair that begins with {reward}feeding ten needy people from the average of what you feed your own family{/reward}, and closes: {idea}guard your oaths{/idea}, so that you may be grateful.
now: Wallahi, I will be there by five. Wallahi, I will pay you back Friday. Allah's name used like a full stop.
