Notice how often you say it. {trap}The name of Allah is not a punctuation mark.{/trap} And notice the kindness: even the repair for a broken oath {reward}begins by feeding someone hungry.{/reward}
old: Saying wallahi is just a way to make people believe me.
new: Allah's name is weighty. I should use it rarely and keep what I swear.
try: For one day, count how many times you swear by Allah, and try to halve it tomorrow.

title: Stay away from it all, that you may succeed.
subtitle: Intoxicants, gambling, idol altars, fortune arrows
then: Abu Hurayrah described how the matter came in stages, and 'Umar kept asking Allah for a clear answer. When this came, Anas said the men at Abu Talhah's house told him to {reward}pour it all out{/reward}, and {idea}it flowed in the streets of Madinah{/idea}. Ibn 'Abbas explained these things as {trap}an abomination of Shaytan's handiwork.{/trap}
now: Forget for a moment what other people do. Picture the Companions emptying their jars the same hour they heard. Now picture your own: the app you open at 1am, the habit that clouds your head. {idea}Avoid it{/idea} ends with a hope, not a scolding: {reward}that you may succeed.{/reward}
old: Some harmful habits are just part of how I relax.
new: What Allah calls Shaytan's work, I can walk away from, and that is where success lies.
try: Identify one thing that clouds your mind or eats your money by chance. Delete, pour, or block it today.

title: So will you not stop?
subtitle: What Shaytan really wants from these things
then: The verse explains the purpose behind these things: Shaytan wants {trap}enmity and hatred between you, and to turn you from remembering Allah and from prayer.{/trap} It ends with a question. When it was recited to 'Umar and he reached {idea}so will you not stop?{/idea}, he said: {reward}We abstained, we abstained.{/reward}
now: The card game that ended with two brothers not speaking. The night out that made you miss Fajr, then Dhuhr. You can see the pattern in your own life: {trap}broken ties and a forgotten prayer.{/trap} The verse asks you directly. {idea}'Umar's answer is still available to you.{/idea}
old: It is harmless as long as I keep it under control.
new: Its real cost is broken relationships and forgetting Allah, which is exactly what Shaytan wants.
try: Look at one habit that makes you miss prayer or fight with family. Answer the verse out loud: I stop.

title: Obey, and be careful. His job was to make it clear.
subtitle: The message is delivered, the choice is yours
then: After the prohibitions, the verse gathers it into one instruction: {idea}obey Allah, obey the Messenger, and beware.{/idea} If people turn away, the Messenger's duty was only {reward}to convey in the clearest way{/reward}, and he did.
now: You know the answer already. It is in the Quran app, on the masjid noticeboard, in the advice your grandmother gave. The excuse {trap}I did not really know{/trap} wears thin. {idea}The message reached you clearly. What happens now is yours.{/idea}
old: If it were really important, someone would have made me do it.
new: The message was made clear. Acting on it is my responsibility.
try: Choose one thing you already know you should do, and stop waiting for someone to remind you.

title: No blame for the past, if you keep rising.
subtitle: Those who died before the ruling came

row.title: taqwa and excellence
sub: Allah loves the doers of good

then: After the prohibition, people asked about Companions who {trap}had died while still drinking, before the ruling came.{/trap} This verse was revealed. The Prophet ﷺ said: {idea}had it been forbidden to them, they would have left it as you have left it.{/idea} The verse then describes {reward}growing in taqwa, belief and good, again and again.{/reward}
now: You learned something new about your deen last month, and you think back with panic about the years before. Allah does not hold you to what you did not yet know. What He asks is {idea}that you keep climbing from here{/idea}: mindful, believing, doing good, then {reward}doing it beautifully.{/reward}
old: Everything I did before I knew better is held against me.
new: What matters is that I keep growing in taqwa and goodness from where I am now.
try: Name one thing you have learned in faith this year. Thank Allah for it instead of regretting the before.

title: The test came within arm's reach.
subtitle: Who fears Allah when no one is watching
then: Muqatil bin Hayyan said this came during the 'Umrah of Hudaybiyah, when {trap}wild game and birds came right into the Muslim camp{/trap}, more than they had ever seen. Ibn 'Abbas said even young animals came close enough to catch by hand. The point was {idea}to show who fears Allah in the unseen{/idea}, in public and in secret.
now: The office is empty. The petty cash box is open. The answers to the online test are one tab away. The ex's message sits unread. {trap}The test is always easiest to fail when it walks right up to you.{/trap} {idea}What you do when no one sees is who you are with Allah.{/idea}
old: If no one will ever know, it does not really count.
new: The moment no one sees is exactly the moment Allah is testing for.
try: Notice one private temptation today that is within easy reach, and leave it for Allah's sake.

title: Taste the weight of the deed, then begin again.
subtitle: Repair, forgiveness for the past, and a warning
then: The verse sets a repair for the pilgrim who breaks this limit, judged by {idea}two just people{/idea}, and adds the reason: {trap}so that he may taste the weight of his deed.{/trap} Then comes mercy: {reward}Allah has pardoned what is past.{/reward} Returning to it after knowing is a different matter.
now: You snapped at your little brother and he went quiet for the rest of the day. Saying sorry costs you something. That cost is good. {trap}It lets you feel the weight{/trap} so you do not do it again. And then {reward}it is over, really over{/reward}. Do not carry it around forever.
old: Making things right should be quick and cost me nothing.
new: Feeling the cost of a wrong helps me stop, and then Allah lets the past go.
try: Repair one small wrong today in a way that costs you a little: time, money, or pride.

title: The sea stays open to you.
subtitle: Even within limits, Allah leaves provision
then: While land hunting is closed to the pilgrim, {reward}the sea and its food stay lawful{/reward}, for residents and travellers. Jabir told of an army so short of food each man got {trap}one date a day{/trap}, until they found a huge fish on the shore and {reward}ate from it for eighteen days{/reward}. The verse ends: be mindful of Allah, {idea}to whom you will be gathered.{/idea}
now: You gave up the haram income stream, or the relationship, or the late-night habit, and now you are staring at the closed door. Look sideways. {reward}Something good is still open{/reward}: a lawful job lead, a friend who calls, a calm evening. {idea}Allah rarely closes a door without leaving a sea.{/idea}
old: Giving something up for Allah leaves me with nothing.
new: When Allah closes one thing, He leaves provision open somewhere else.
try: Write down one lawful good thing in your life that you have been overlooking.

title: The Ka'bah as a pillar of safety for people.
subtitle: Sacred places and times that hold life together
then: Ibn Kathir's editors note his tafsir is missing here and summarise At-Tabari: Allah made the Ka'bah {reward}a refuge of safety for people with no ruler to stop the strong oppressing the weak{/reward}. The sacred months and marked offerings did the same. This shows that {idea}Allah knows all that is in the heavens and earth.{/idea}
now: Think of the one place where everyone in your family drops their arguments: grandmother's house, the masjid on Eid morning. Allah gave the world {idea}fixed sacred places and times{/idea} so that {reward}the weak have somewhere safe{/reward}. Be the person who keeps that peace, not the one who breaks it.
old: Sacred places and times are just traditions.
new: Allah set sacred places and times so people, especially the weak, could be safe.
try: Make one space or time in your home this week where no one argues, and protect it.

title: Severe in penalty, and Forgiving, Merciful.
subtitle: Holding both truths at once

row.title: both together
sub: fear that returns, hope that acts

then: After the limits on hunting, the Sacred House and the sacred months, the verse asks people to {idea}know two things together{/idea}: Allah is {trap}severe in penalty{/trap}, and He is {reward}Forgiving and Merciful{/reward}. Neither one is complete alone.
now: Some days you feel so guilty you stop praying altogether. Other days you think Allah is forgiving, so why worry. {idea}Both are half the picture.{/idea} Fear is meant to turn you around. {reward}Hope is meant to welcome you back.{/reward}
old: Allah is either strict or forgiving, depending on my mood.
new: He is both. Fear keeps me careful and hope keeps me coming back.
try: Today, ask for forgiveness for one thing and thank Allah for one mercy, side by side.

title: He delivered it. Allah sees what you show and hide.
subtitle: The message is clear, the heart is seen

row.title: Allah
sub: knows what you show and hide

then: The verse closes this passage of rulings with two facts. The Messenger's ﷺ duty {idea}was only to convey{/idea}, and that is done. And {idea}Allah knows whatever you reveal and whatever you conceal.{/idea} The rest is between each person and Allah.
now: Your public self: the polite comment, the good post, the smile at the masjid. Your private self: the search history, the resentment you never voice. {trap}People only get the first one.{/trap} {idea}Allah sees both, and loves it when they match.{/idea}
old: As long as I look good outside, the rest is my business.
new: Allah sees the hidden as clearly as the shown, so I want them to match.
try: Pick one gap between your public and private self and close it a little today.

title: A lot of bad does not equal a little good.
subtitle: Quantity is not the measure
then: The Prophet ﷺ is told to say that bad and good are never equal, {trap}even if the abundance of the bad impresses you.{/trap} Ibn Kathir explains: {reward}the little that is lawful is better than the abundant that is evil.{/reward} People of understanding let the lawful be enough.
now: Your friend's side hustle makes triple your salary, and you know how. The influencer has a million followers for content you would not show your mother. {trap}The size of it pulls at you.{/trap} The verse says: {idea}stop counting. Weigh.{/idea}
old: If there is a lot of it, it must be worth something.
new: A small amount of good outweighs a mountain of what is bad.
try: Look at your income or your feed. Name one thing that is big but not good, and step back from it.

title: Some questions are better left unasked.
subtitle: Mercy hidden in what was left unsaid

row.title: no
sub: had I said yes, you could not bear it

then: When Hajj was made a duty, people asked the Prophet ﷺ {trap}is it every year?{/trap} He stayed silent until the third time, then said {reward}no, and had I said yes, it would have become required and you could not bear it.{/reward} A hadith in the tafsir says Allah left some matters without rulings {idea}out of mercy, not forgetfulness.{/idea}
now: You keep checking your partner's phone. You keep asking what people really said about you at the wedding. You keep digging until you find something that hurts. Some answers {trap}will only cause you distress{/trap}. {idea}Not every door needs to be opened.{/idea}
old: Knowing more is always better.
new: Some questions only bring distress, and leaving them is a mercy.
try: Notice one question you keep digging into that only hurts you. Let it go for today.

title: They got their answers and walked away anyway.
subtitle: Asking without wanting to follow
then: Ibn Kathir explains that people before had asked such questions and {idea}were given clear answers{/idea}, but {trap}did not believe them{/trap}. They had asked not for guidance, but {trap}to mock and defy.{/trap} The answers only made their refusal plain.
now: The question in the comments that is really a trap. The "just asking" in the family WhatsApp that is really a jab. Before you ask the imam, your parent or Google, check: {idea}if I get the answer, will I follow it?{/idea}
old: Asking questions is always a sign of a sincere seeker.
new: A question asked without the will to follow can push me further away.
try: Before your next religious question, decide first that you will act on the answer.

title: Allah never made those rules.
subtitle: Customs invented and credited to Allah
then: Before Islam, Arabs had dedicated certain camels to idols and banned riding or milking them. Sa'id bin al-Musayyib explained each name. Ibn Kathir says 'Amr bin Luhay of Khuza'ah {trap}was the first to change the religion of Ibrahim{/trap} and start such rituals. The verse says plainly: {idea}Allah did not appoint any of these.{/idea}
now: The rule that a widow must not wear colour for years. The idea that a girl who studies is less marriageable. The old aunt who says "this is our religion". Ask gently: {idea}did Allah actually say this?{/idea} {trap}Custom wearing the clothes of religion{/trap} is what this verse undoes.
old: If my family has always done it, it must be part of the deen.
new: Only what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ taught is the deen. Customs must be checked against it.
try: Pick one rule you grew up with and find out today whether it comes from the Quran or Sunnah.

title: Enough for us is what our fathers did.
subtitle: When inheritance replaces guidance
then: When told {idea}come to what Allah revealed and to the Messenger{/idea}, they answered: {trap}what we found our fathers doing is enough for us.{/trap} The verse asks back: even if their fathers had no knowledge and no guidance? It comes straight after the invented animal customs of the verse before.
now: "That is how we do it in this family." You have said it about weddings, about money, about how you treat the women in the house. Your parents are owed love and respect. {idea}They are not owed the place of revelation.{/idea} Honour them by {reward}keeping the good and quietly fixing the rest.{/reward}
old: Questioning how my family does things is disrespectful.
new: I can love my elders and still follow guidance over habit.
try: Name one family habit you follow without knowing why. Look into it with an open mind this week.

title: Tend your own soul first.
subtitle: Responsibility for yourself, without abandoning others

row.title: reform yourself
sub: and still change what you see

then: Ibn Kathir says Allah tells the believers to {idea}reform themselves first{/idea}, and that one who does so is not harmed by others' wrongdoing, even relatives. Abu Bakr once stood and warned people they were {trap}reading this verse the wrong way{/trap}, quoting the Prophet ﷺ: if people see evil and do not change it, punishment may cover them all.
now: You get absorbed in what everyone else is doing wrong: your sibling's choices, your colleague's shortcuts, the comments under a post. Meanwhile your own prayer is slipping. Start with {idea}your own heart{/idea}. That is not the same as {trap}shrugging at wrong{/trap}. It is fixing yourself so your voice carries.
old: Either I focus on others' wrongs, or I mind my own business completely.
new: I reform myself first, and from there I can still help others kindly.
try: Before commenting on anyone else's faults today, fix one small thing in your own routine.

title: Even for a relative, we will not sell our oath.
subtitle: Witnessing a dying person's wishes faithfully

picture.label: At a deathbed on a journey

then: The verse covers a hard moment: death approaching on a journey, a will being made, two witnesses present. If doubted, they swear after the prayer: {idea}we will not exchange this for any gain, even for a near relative, and we will not hide the testimony of Allah.{/idea} Ibn Kathir notes it is called Allah's testimony {reward}to show how much it is worth.{/reward}
now: Your uncle is dying. He tells you, quietly, what he wants done with his savings. Later, the family argues, and your side would gain if you remembered it a little differently. {trap}A small bend for family{/trap} feels almost loyal. The verse says: {idea}not even for family.{/idea}
old: Bending the truth a little to help my family is loyalty.
new: What I witness is a trust from Allah. I will not trade it, even for family.
try: If you are holding anyone's wishes or words in trust, write them down accurately today.

title: When witnesses cheat, the rightful step up.
subtitle: Correcting false testimony with truthful testimony
then: If the witnesses are found to have {trap}cheated or stolen from the estate{/trap}, Ibn Kathir explains, two of the nearest rightful heirs swear in their place. Their oath includes a line that matters: {idea}we have not transgressed, or we would be among the wrongdoers.{/idea} Even the correction must be honest.
now: Someone lied about you at work, and you finally get your chance to set the record straight. It is tempting to {trap}add a few extra charges while you are at it{/trap}. The heirs in this verse swear they have not overstepped. {idea}Your correction has to be as true as you wish theirs had been.{/idea}
old: Once someone wrongs me, I am free to say whatever I like about them.
new: Even when correcting a lie, I must not cross into one myself.
try: Next time you tell the story of someone who wronged you, tell only what you know for sure.

title: A system that makes honesty more likely.
subtitle: Why oaths and checks protect the truth
then: Ibn Kathir explains the wisdom: swearing by Allah, whom they revere, and the chance that {trap}the heirs' oaths may overturn theirs{/trap}, both push witnesses to tell the truth as it is. The verse ends with the core: {idea}fear Allah and listen.{/idea}
now: The family business with no written records. The group trip money that "we will sort out later". Good people still forget and still get tempted. {idea}Writing it down, having a witness, being accountable{/idea} is not distrust. {reward}It protects everyone, including you.{/reward}
old: Asking for records or witnesses means I do not trust people.
new: Clear checks plus fear of Allah protect everyone's honesty, including mine.
try: Write down one money arrangement you have with family or friends and share it with them.

title: Even the messengers will say: we have no knowledge.
subtitle: The Day when only Allah knows what was hidden

row.title: I know their hearts
sub: I can tell what they meant

then: Allah will gather the messengers and ask how their people responded. Mujahid and others said they answer {trap}we have no knowledge{/trap} out of the awe of that Day. Ibn 'Abbas explained it as respect: {idea}our knowledge saw only what people did outwardly; You know what was in their hearts.{/idea}
now: You are sure you know why your friend did not invite you, why your sister-in-law said that, why that man at the masjid frowned. The best of humanity will say {idea}we only saw the outside.{/idea} Maybe {trap}you do not know their hearts either.{/trap}
old: I can usually tell what people really meant.
new: I see what people do. Only Allah knows why.
try: Think of one person whose motives you have judged. Give them one good excuse today.

title: Remember My favour on you and your mother.
subtitle: Every miracle of 'Isa, by Allah's permission
then: On the Day of Resurrection, Allah will remind 'Isa of His favours: {reward}Jibril's support, speaking as a baby to clear his mother's name{/reward}, the Book and wisdom, the clay bird, healing, raising the dead. Every one is followed by {idea}by My permission.{/idea} Ibn Kathir notes that Allah also saved him from those who rejected him and tried to kill him.
now: The promotion, the recovery after surgery, the child who finally started talking. You worked hard, the doctors were good. But {idea}by His permission{/idea} belongs after each one. List them. {reward}Remembering favours is how gratitude starts.{/reward}
old: My successes come from my effort and skill.
new: Every good thing I do happens by Allah's permission, even the miracles of prophets.
try: Write a list of five favours in your life and add by Allah's permission after each.

title: Allah put faith in their hearts, and they answered.
subtitle: The disciples' response to inspiration

row.title: Allah inspired
sub: believe in Me and My messenger

then: This is another favour on 'Isa: {reward}companions who believed with him.{/reward} Al-Hasan al-Basri said Allah inspired them, and As-Suddi said {idea}He put it in their hearts{/idea}. They replied: {reward}we believe, so bear witness that we are Muslims.{/reward}
now: That moment you suddenly felt the pull to pray again, after months. That verse that hit you at a funeral. You might think you decided. {idea}Allah placed it in your heart.{/idea} Your part is to answer like the disciples did: {reward}I believe, bear witness.{/reward}
old: My faith is something I built on my own.
new: Allah puts faith in the heart. My part is to answer it.
try: Thank Allah today for the moment He first turned your heart toward Him, if you can remember it.

title: Can your Lord send us a table from heaven?
subtitle: The request that gave this surah its name
then: This is the story of al-Ma'idah, the table that names the surah. Some scholars said the disciples were poor and wanted daily food to help them worship. Ibn Kathir explains 'Isa's reply: {idea}be mindful of Allah, do not ask for this, for it may become a trial for you; trust Allah for your provision.{/idea}
now: You pray: if You really hear me, give me a sign. The job offer, the test result, a message from them. {trap}Asking for proof can turn into a test you might fail.{/trap} 'Isa's answer still works: {idea}be mindful of Allah, and trust Him with your provision.{/idea}
old: If Allah showed me a clear sign, my faith would be strong.
new: Trust comes first. Demanding signs can become its own trial.
try: Make one dua today without asking for a sign, just trusting that He heard.

title: Not just hunger: hearts wanting to be sure.
subtitle: Four reasons the disciples gave
then: After 'Isa told them to be mindful of Allah, the disciples explained themselves. Ibn Kathir lists it: {reward}we need to eat from it{/reward}, we want {idea}our faith to grow stronger when we see it come down{/idea}, to know {idea}you told us the truth{/idea}, and to bear witness that it is a sign from Allah.
now: You believe, but some nights at 2am your heart is restless and you want to feel sure. That is not the end of your faith. {idea}Hearts ask to be reassured.{/idea} Feed that request with what reassures: {reward}the Quran, dhikr, and people of faith around you.{/reward}
old: If I ever want reassurance, my faith must be weak.
new: Wanting my heart to be at rest is human. Faith can grow with reassurance.
try: Tonight, when your heart is restless, read one page of Quran with its meaning before you scroll.

title: A festival for the first of us and the last.
subtitle: 'Isa's dua, ending with: You are the best provider

row.title: a festival
sub: for first and last of us

row.title: O Allah, our Lord
sub: for all generations, ending in praise

then: 'Isa turned the request into a dua: {idea}O Allah, our Lord{/idea}, send us a table to be {reward}a festival for the first and last of us, and a sign from You{/reward}. As-Suddi said the day it came down would be honoured by them and those after them; Sufyan ath-Thawri said a day of prayer. He ended: {reward}You are the best of providers.{/reward}
now: You ask Allah for the rent money, for the visa, for the scan to be clear. Try asking the way 'Isa did: begin with {idea}O Allah, our Lord{/idea}, ask for good that {reward}reaches your children and theirs{/reward}, and end by praising Him as the best provider.
old: Dua is just telling Allah what I need right now.
new: The best dua names Him, asks widely, and ends in praise.
try: Make one dua today that starts with Allahumma Rabbana and ends with: You are the best of providers.

title: I will send it. A great sign brings great responsibility.
subtitle: The answer, and the weight that came with it
then: Allah accepted 'Isa's dua: {reward}I will send it down to you.{/reward} But a clear sign leaves no excuse, so whoever denied it afterwards faced {trap}a punishment like no other of their time.{/trap} Ibn Jarir reported that when some {trap}took food secretly, saying it might not come tomorrow{/trap}, the table was lifted.
now: You prayed for the job, and it came. You begged for your mother's recovery, and she is home. Now comes the quiet part: {idea}do you live like someone whose prayer was answered?{/idea} Or do you {trap}hoard and forget{/trap}, as if it might not come again?
old: Once Allah gives me what I asked, the matter is closed.
new: An answered prayer is a trust. Gratitude and trust should grow after it.
try: Recall one prayer Allah answered for you. Do one thing today to thank Him for it.

title: It was not for me to claim what is not mine.
subtitle: 'Isa's answer on the Day of Resurrection

row.title: Allah asks
sub: did you tell people to worship you?

row.title: Glory be to You
sub: I had no right to that

then: On the Day of Resurrection Allah will ask 'Isa whether he told people to worship him and his mother. Abu Hurayrah narrated that {reward}Allah Himself will teach 'Isa his reply{/reward}: {idea}Glory be to You! It was not for me to say what I had no right to.{/idea} He adds: You know what is in my self, and I do not know what is in Yours.
now: People praise you at work, call you the one who fixes everything. Your family treats your word as final. It is easy to {trap}take a role that is not yours{/trap}. 'Isa, who raised the dead by Allah's permission, said: {idea}it was not for me.{/idea} Know where your place ends.
old: If people honour me, I can accept whatever title they give.
new: Even the greatest servant refuses any place that belongs to Allah alone.
try: When someone praises you today, quietly say alhamdulillah and give the credit back to Allah.

title: I was a witness while I was among them.
subtitle: Responsibility while present, Allah's watch after

row.title: only what You said
sub: worship Allah, my Lord and yours

then: 'Isa says he only told them {idea}worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord{/idea}, and was a witness over them only while he was with them. Ibn 'Abbas narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said that on the Day, when some of his followers are taken away for what they changed after him, {reward}he will say what the righteous servant 'Isa said.{/reward}
now: Your children will grow up and make choices you never taught. Your students will forget half of what you said. You answer for {idea}what you said and modelled while you were there{/idea}. After that, {reward}Allah is the Watcher.{/reward} Teach well now, and let go of what you cannot control.
old: If the people I raised go wrong later, it is all my fault.
new: I answer for what I taught while present. After that, Allah watches over them.
try: Teach one small good thing to a child or younger person today, clearly and kindly.

title: They are Your servants. If You forgive, You are Mighty, Wise.
subtitle: Handing people's fate back to Allah
then: 'Isa does not plead or condemn. He returns the matter to Allah: {idea}they are Your servants; if You forgive them, You are the Almighty, the All-Wise.{/idea} Ibn Kathir says all matters return to Allah, and calls this verse {reward}of tremendous value{/reward}. The Prophet ﷺ will repeat it on the Day.
now: You have decided where certain people will end up: the uncle who left prayer, the friend who left the deen, the stranger online. 'Isa, a prophet, would not decide it. {idea}They are His servants.{/idea} {reward}Leave their end to Him{/reward}, and keep praying for them.
old: I can tell who will be punished and who will be forgiven.
new: People's final fate belongs to Allah. My part is to hope and to pray for them.
try: Make dua tonight for someone you had judged, using 'Isa's words: they are Your servants.

title: The Day when truthfulness finally pays.
subtitle: Allah pleased with them, and they with Him
then: After 'Isa's honest answers, Allah says: {idea}this is the Day the truthful benefit from their truthfulness.{/idea} Ibn 'Abbas said: the Day when tawhid benefits those who believed in it. Their reward: Gardens forever, and {reward}Allah pleased with them and they with Him{/reward}. Ibn Kathir calls it the success beyond which there is none greater.
now: Telling the truth about the dent in the rental car. Admitting to your manager you missed the deadline. Being honest with Allah in sujood about who you really are. In this world truth sometimes costs you. {reward}There is a Day when only truth pays.{/reward}
old: Being completely honest often just loses me things.
new: Truthfulness may cost me here, but it is the only thing that pays on that Day.
try: Tell the full truth today in one situation where you would usually soften it.

title: Everything belongs to Him, and He can do all things.
subtitle: The final line of the surah

row.title: mine
sub: my house, my career, my plans

row.title: His
sub: entrusted to me for a while

then: The surah of covenants, limits and the table from heaven closes on one fact: {idea}to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and everything in them.{/idea} Ibn Kathir: He created, owns and runs everything, with no partner. 'Abdullah bin 'Amr said Al-Ma'idah was {reward}the last surah revealed.{/reward}
now: The house keys in your pocket, the salary, the children asleep in the next room. You call them mine. {idea}They are His, lent to you for a while.{/idea} That is not a loss. It means {reward}the One who owns everything is also looking after it all, and after you.{/reward}
old: What I have built and earned is mine to keep.
new: Everything belongs to Allah and He can do anything, so I hold it lightly and trust Him.
try: Look around your room and say: all of this is Yours, Allah. Thank you for lending it.
